record.boundary_rationale: Core territory = the middle Mekong valley, from the Phongsaly/Sipsong Panna fringe in the north to Champasak in the south, bounded east by the Annamite Range crest (frontier with Dai Viet) and west by a strip of the eastern Khorat Plateau, whose control by Lan Xang Ayutthaya acknowledged after Fa Ngum's 1356-57 campaigns. The ring encloses both capitals (Luang Prabang 1354-1560, Vientiane 1560-1707) and the Lao mueang heartland. It deliberately excludes the outer tributary zones (Sipsong Panna proper, the Lanna fringe, the deep Khorat Plateau, Cambodian marches below the Khone rapids) whose allegiance fluctuated in the mandala system. 10-point counterclockwise ring, longitude span 6.2 degrees.

record.chain_notes: Predecessor: the Lao-Tai mueang of the middle Mekong, chiefly Mueang Sua (Xieng Dong Xieng Thong, today Luang Prabang), unified VIOLENTLY by Fa Ngum in 1349-1354 with Khmer (Angkor) military backing; coronation dated June 1354 (some sources 1353). Successors: 1707 partition - after the succession crisis following Sourigna Vongsa's death in 1694, his grandson Kingkitsarat (exiled in Sipsong Panna, crowned rival king at Luang Prabang in 1705) and Sai Ong Hue (nephew line, ruling Vientiane with Vietnamese Trinh backing) divided the kingdom in 1707: Kingdom of Luang Prabang (north) and Kingdom of Vientiane (center-south). The split was a negotiated/de facto division after an armed standoff, NOT a battlefield conquest - mark the 1707 transition as essentially peaceful partition. The Kingdom of Champasak then separated from Vientiane's sphere in 1713 after a southern rebellion (first king Nokasad), completing the three-way division. All three successor kingdoms were reduced to Siamese vassalage in 1778-79.
record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-002: Lan Xang was founded by military conquest - Fa Ngum, backed by a Khmer (Angkor) army, subjugated Mueang Sua and the middle-Mekong mueang in 1349-1354, and chronicle accounts record the brutality of his campaigns. ETHICS-002: The Burmese Toungoo dynasty under Bayinnaung invaded in 1563-65 and 1568-70, and Burmese forces captured and sacked Vientiane in 1574, deporting captives (including the heir) to Pegu and holding Lan Xang as a vassal until c. 1591; in 1479 Dai Viet under Le Thanh Tong invaded and sacked Luang Prabang in the 'White Elephant War'. Warfare in this region was manpower warfare: victorious armies - Burmese, Siamese, Vietnamese and Lao alike - routinely deported whole populations as forced labor, and Lan Xang's economy also rested on corvee and slave-raiding of upland peoples (kha), a term itself derogatory. ETHICS-001: the primary name is the attested Lao form ອານາຈັກລ້ານຊ້າງ; the founding ceremonial name Lan Xang Hom Khao ('Million Elephants and the White Parasol') is attested in the Lao chronicles. Later French colonial historiography reframed Lan Xang as a proto-'Laos' to legitimize the 1893 protectorate, a teleology modern scholarship rejects. Internally, the Theravada Buddhist state (formalized under Photisarath, whose 1527 edicts suppressed indigenous spirit/phi worship) marginalized non-Buddhist highland religions as policy, even as Vientiane under Sourigna Vongsa (1637-1694) became a monastic learning center drawing monks from Siam and Cambodia. Lao-authored historiography (Souneth Phothisane's annotated translation of the Nidan Khun Borom chronicle) is cited alongside Western academic sources per the non-Western-historiography requirement.
record.caveats: Founding year varies by source: chronicles date Fa Ngum's coronation to June 1354 (used here, matching Wikidata), but his conquest of Mueang Sua is dated 1353 and several references (including Wikipedia's infobox) use 1353. Lan Xang was a mandala polity of tributary mueang, not a territorial state with linear borders: the polygon approximates the core middle-Mekong valley and cannot capture fluctuating tributary zones (Sipsong Panna fringe, deep Khorat Plateau, Muang Phuan/Xieng Khouang - which simultaneously paid tribute to Vietnam). Control west of the Mekong on the Khorat Plateau varied over the kingdom's life. The 1707 end date marks the de facto two-way partition; the three-way division completed only in 1713 with Champasak. Events before c. 1500 rest on chronicle traditions (Nithan Khun Borom and successors) compiled and copied later, carrying legendary elements - hence confidence 0.7 despite well-attested later dates.

territory_changes.description: The Podgorica Assembly (in session 24-29 November 1918), convened under Serbian army presence with an irregular electoral procedure, deposed King Nikola I Petrović-Njegoš and proclaimed unconditional union with Serbia. The Greens' Christmas Uprising against the annexation (Cetinje, 7 January 1919, led by Krsto Popović) was crushed by Serbian troops and pro-union White militias; guerrilla resistance and reprisals continued into the mid-1920s. Montenegrin and part of Western historiography (Pavlović 2008) call this an annexation; Serbian unification historiography calls it a voluntary union.

territory_changes.region: All South Slav lands (Serbia, Montenegro, former Habsburg South Slav territories)
territory_changes.description: 1 December 1918: Regent Aleksandar Karađorđević proclaimed the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, uniting the Kingdom of Serbia (with newly absorbed Montenegro) and the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs formed from the collapsed Austria-Hungary — a negotiated unification (Corfu Declaration 1917, National Council address), not a treaty in the strict sense.

Treaty of Rapallo (12 November 1920): the Kingdom ceded Istria, Zadar and several islands to Italy; roughly half a million South Slavs (Slovenes, Croats) came under Italian rule and subsequent forced Italianization. Rijeka went to Italy by the 1924 Treaty of Rome, with Sušak remaining Yugoslav.

Axis invasion from 6 April 1941, opened by Nazi Germany's terror bombing of Belgrade that killed thousands of civilians; unconditional surrender on 17 April 1941. Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, Hungary and Bulgaria partitioned the country, installing the Ustaša-run Independent State of Croatia (10 April 1941), occupied Serbia, the Italian Governorate of Montenegro and the Province of Ljubljana.

record.chain_notes: Predecessors: (1) Kingdom of Serbia (Краљевина Србија) — merged by the proclamation of 1 December 1918, peaceful and negotiated with the National Council in Zagreb; Serbia itself descends from the Ottoman-era Principality of Serbia (autonomy 1830, independence 1878, kingdom 1882), linking this record to the Ottoman-era Serbian chain. (2) Kingdom of Montenegro (Краљевина Црна Гора) — absorbed via the contested Podgorica Assembly resolution of late November 1918, held under Serbian military presence; the transition's aftermath was violent (Christmas Uprising of January 1919 crushed by Serbian troops and White militias; guerrilla warfare into the mid-1920s). (3) State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs (29 Oct - 1 Dec 1918, internationally unrecognized) — peaceful merger. Successor: socialist Yugoslavia — Democratic Federal Yugoslavia proclaimed by AVNOJ, becoming the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia on 29 November 1945 when the Constituent Assembly abolished the monarchy. That transition was violent: Axis invasion and partition (April 1941), four years of occupation, genocide and liberation/civil war ending in Partisan victory (1945). year_end=1941 marks the de facto territorial end (partition); de jure royal continuity via the London government-in-exile lasted until 29 November 1945.
record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-002: Montenegro's entry into the new state was not a free union: the Podgorica Assembly (24-29 November 1918), convened under Serbian military presence with an irregular electoral procedure, deposed King Nikola I and proclaimed unconditional union with Serbia, and the Greens' Christmas Uprising (January 1919) was suppressed by the Serbian army and pro-union White militias, with executions, house-burnings and guerrilla fighting into the mid-1920s; Montenegrin historiography (Pavlović 2008) documents this as annexation, Serbian unification historiography as voluntary union — both readings are recorded, not arbitrated. ETHICS-002: On 6 January 1929 King Aleksandar I Karađorđević abolished the constitution, dissolved parliament and banned national and ethnic parties (the 6 January Dictatorship), months after Croat Peasant Party leader Stjepan Radić was fatally shot by a Serb deputy inside the Belgrade parliament (June 1928); the 1929 renaming to Yugoslavia imposed a unitary identity that suppressed Croat, Macedonian and Albanian national expression — Vardar Macedonia was administered as 'South Serbia' and interwar agrarian colonization settled Serb colonists on lands of Albanians and Turks in Kosovo and Macedonia. ETHICS-002: The state ended through external violence: Nazi Germany, with Italy, Hungary and Bulgaria, invaded on 6 April 1941, opening with the Luftwaffe terror bombing of Belgrade that killed thousands of civilians; after the capitulation of 17 April 1941 the invaders partitioned the country and installed the Ustaša Independent State of Croatia, which carried out genocide against Serbs, Roma and Jews. ETHICS-001: the primary name is the attested founding Serbian-Cyrillic form; the 1918-1920 proclamation form 'Краљевство Срба, Хрвата и Словенаца' and the 1929 'Краљевина Југославија' are recorded as period variants rather than replacing it.
record.caveats: year_end=1941 is a documented editorial choice: effective territorial existence ended with the Axis invasion (6 April 1941) and capitulation/partition (17 April 1941), while the royal government-in-exile in London preserved de jure continuity until the monarchy was abolished on 29 November 1945 — users needing the de jure span should read 1918-1945 (Wikidata gives dissolution 29 Nov 1945). Wikidata splits the polity into Q15102440 (Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, 1918-1929) and Q191077 (Kingdom of Yugoslavia, 1929-1945); Q191077 is given here because it anchors the article covering the whole state — both QIDs verified. The boundary is a 13-point approximation of the stable 1924-1941 borders and cannot resolve enclaves (Italian Zadar) or the Rijeka/Sušak split. Sources differ on the exact day of the Podgorica Assembly's union resolution (26 vs 28 November 1918); the record therefore cites the session range 24-29 November. The 1918-1920 official form was 'Краљевство' (changed to 'Краљевина' on 15 July 1920). Confidence 0.75 reflects certain dates and verified QID but an approximate boundary and the contested Montenegro chronology.

record.boundary_rationale: Core territory only: the Tonle Sap-Lower Mekong axis around the successive Middle-Period capitals (Chaktomuk/Phnom Penh, Longvek, Oudong), approximating 17th-century central Cambodia. Deliberately excludes the Mekong Delta (Kampuchea Krom), progressively detached by Nguyen Vietnam 1698-1757, and does not track Siam's 1794 seizure of Battambang/Siem Reap or the Vietnamese annexation of 1834-1841. Actual control fluctuated heavily with Siamese and Vietnamese invasions; the polygon is an honest approximation, not a legal border.
record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-002: The period opened and closed with violence and coercion. Ayutthaya (Siam) sacked the Khmer capital Yasodharapura (Angkor) around 1431, and on 3 January 1594 King Naresuan of Ayutthaya stormed and looted the capital Longvek, deporting much of its population — remembered in Khmer tradition as a national catastrophe. ETHICS-002: The Nguyen lords of Vietnam progressively annexed Kampuchea Krom (the Mekong Delta): in 1698 Nguyen Huu Canh administratively detached Prey Nokor (renamed Sai Gon) from Cambodia, and by 1757 the entire delta was absorbed, leaving the Khmer Krom a dispossessed minority under Vietnamese rule to this day. ETHICS-002: In 1834-1841 Emperor Minh Mang annexed Cambodia outright as the Vietnamese province of Tran Tay, installed Queen Ang Mey as a puppet and imposed forced Vietnamization, until a Khmer rebellion and Siamese intervention restored King Ang Duong under joint Siamese-Vietnamese suzerainty (formalized 1845-1847); Siam separately seized Battambang and Siem Reap provinces in 1794. ETHICS-002: The 11 August 1863 'protection' treaty with France was signed by King Norodom under French naval-diplomatic pressure and as an escape from Siamese-Vietnamese domination — a colonial protectorate, not a partnership of equals. ETHICS-001: The primary name is the attested Khmer endonym កម្ពុជា (Kampuchea, attested since the Baksei Chamkrong inscription, 947 CE, and throughout the Middle Period); 'Cambodia', 'Camboja' and 'Cambodge' are European exonyms kept in name_variants. The 'Dark Age' framing (reflected in the Khmer Wikidata label យុគអន្ធកាលនៃកម្ពុជា) is contested historiography — Vickery and later scholarship show an era of reorientation toward maritime trade, not simple decay.

territory_changes.description: Ayutthaya (Siam) captured and sacked the Khmer capital Yasodharapura (Angkor); the royal court shifted south to Chaktomuk (Phnom Penh), founding the Middle Period. Conventional date — the exact nature and year of the Siamese intervention are debated (Vickery 1977), and Angkor's abandonment was gradual.

King Naresuan of Ayutthaya stormed, looted and destroyed the capital Longvek on 3 January 1594, ending the Siamese-Cambodian War of 1591-1594; population deported, Cambodia reduced to intermittent Siamese vassalage. Court later re-established at Oudong (1618).

The Nguyen lords commissioned Nguyen Huu Canh to organize Prey Nokor (renamed Sai Gon) under Vietnamese administration, de facto detaching it from Cambodia; by 1757 the whole delta (Psar Dek/Sa Dec, Moat Chrouk/Chau Doc) was absorbed into Vietnam, dispossessing the Khmer Krom.

King Norodom signed the French protectorate treaty on 11 August 1863 under French naval-diplomatic pressure, ending the Siamese-Vietnamese dual vassalage; the monarchy survived but power passed to a French resident. Successor chain leads into French Indochina (federation formed 1887).

record.chain_notes: Predecessor: Khmer Empire — link at 1431, violent (Ayutthayan sack of Yasodharapura/Angkor; conventional chronicle-based date, gradual abandonment per recent geoarchaeology). Successor: French protectorate of Cambodia / French Indochina — link at 1863, formally peaceful (protectorate treaty signed by King Norodom on 11 August 1863) but concluded under French gunboat-diplomacy coercion; monarchy retained. Note: Oudong formally remained the royal seat until 1866, when Norodom moved the court to Phnom Penh under the protectorate; 1863 is used as the entity end (sovereignty transfer). Internal capital sequence: Chaktomuk/Phnom Penh (from ~1431), Longvek (~1525-1594, destroyed by Ayutthaya), Srei Santhor interlude, Oudong (1618-1863).
record.caveats: Start date 1431 is conventional: the chronicles' account of the Siamese capture of Angkor is of uncertain date and nature (Vickery 1977), and geoarchaeology shows gradual, not catastrophic, abandonment of Angkor. Boundaries fluctuated drastically across four centuries; the polygon shows the ~17th-century core Tonle Sap-Lower Mekong axis and does not track the staged loss of the Mekong Delta (1698-1757), Siam's seizure of Battambang/Siem Reap (1794), or the Vietnamese Tran Tay annexation (1834-1841), during which the kingdom briefly ceased to exist as a polity. Wikidata Q4919413 models this as a time interval/historical country rather than a formally named state; the primary name uses the attested endonym កម្ពុជា with a parenthetical disambiguator because the unqualified modern name is already assigned to the Kingdom of Cambodia entity (Babylon-split precedent). Khmer historiography of the period rests heavily on later royal chronicles of uneven reliability, hence confidence 0.7.

verdict.notes: All 7 checks pass. (1) NAME: កម្ពុជា is the standard Khmer spelling of Kampuchea; the "Kambuja" endonym is indeed attested in the Baksei Chamkrong inscription (947 CE) per Names of Cambodia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_Cambodia). Minor nuance, not an error: the 947 inscription is in Sanskrit ("Kambuja/Kambujadesa"), so the modern Khmer orthography កម្ពុជា is the descendant form rather than the literal 947 glyphs — the record's phrasing is an acceptable simplification. The (Longvek-Oudong) disambiguator is explicitly documented in caveats. (2) DATES: 1431-1863 matches mainstream historiography (fall of Angkor to French protectorate) and the record properly flags 1431 as conventional per Vickery. (3) QID: Wikidata Q4919413 verified by direct fetch — label "Post-Angkor Cambodia", instance of time interval + historical country, inception 1431, end 1863, subdivided into Chaktomuk/Longvek/Srey Santhor/Oudong eras, exactly matching the record's internal capital sequence. (4) CAPITAL: Oudong gazetteer position is 11.8000, 104.7500 (latitude.to); record's 11.8239, 104.7425 is ~2.7 km away, consistent with the Phnom Oudong royal-necropolis hill — right city, right country. (5) BOUNDARY: bbox is lon 102.6-106.5, lat 10.4-14.2 — central Cambodia / Tonle Sap-lower Mekong axis; no antimeridian crossing (width 3.9 deg), size appropriate for a kingdom, matches the stated rationale of excluding the Mekong Delta. Passes under the lenient standard. (6) SOURCES: Khin Sok 1991 verified on the EFEO publisher page (publications.efeo.fr/en/livres/192_...); Mak Phoeun 1995 verified via EFEO catalog + Persee review + Gallica digitization; Chandler 2008 and Vickery 1977 are canonical works. territory_changes.description: After defeats by Voortrekker commandos in the Transvaal (Vegkop 1836, Mosega/eGabeni 1837), Mzilikazi's Khumalo-led Ndebele crossed the Limpopo and settled the southwestern Zimbabwean plateau (c. 1838-1840), displacing and forcibly incorporating local Kalanga and Rozvi-Shona communities.

Ndebele forces defeated the Rozvi Mutinhima house; the remaining Rozvi royal houses, leaderless since Nyamazana's Ngoni sacked Danamombe and killed Changamire Chirisamhuru c. 1835, submitted one by one c. 1839-1840 and were reduced to tributary status.

territory_changes.description: Rudd Concession (30 Oct 1888): Lobengula granted exclusive mineral rights to Cecil Rhodes's agents Charles Rudd, Rochfort Maguire and Francis Thompson for 100 pounds per lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles, 100,000 cartridges and a Zambezi steamboat. Interpreter Charles Helm's mistranslation and the exclusion of verbal assurances (max ten diggers, subject to Ndebele law) from the written English text made it fraudulent; Lobengula repudiated it and protested to Queen Victoria without effect. It became the legal basis of the British South Africa Company's royal charter (Oct 1889) and the 1890 Pioneer Column occupation of Mashonaland.

First Matabele War: British South Africa Company columns using Maxim guns killed roughly 1,500 Ndebele at the Shangani (25 Oct 1893) and about 2,500 at Bembesi (1 Nov 1893) against single-digit company battle deaths; Lobengula burned koBulawayo and fled north; the BSAC occupied Bulawayo on 4 Nov 1893 and seized Ndebele land and cattle. Lobengula died in flight, probably of smallpox, on 22/23 Jan 1894.

record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-002: The kingdom was destroyed by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company in the First Matabele War (October 1893 - January 1894): company Maxim guns, used here in battle for the first time, killed roughly 1,500 Ndebele at the Shangani (25 Oct 1893) and about 2,500 at Bembesi (1 Nov 1893) against single-digit company battle deaths; koBulawayo was occupied on 4 November 1893, Lobengula died in flight in January 1894, and the company's Victoria Agreement 'loot' terms promised each volunteer about 6,000 acres of seized Ndebele land plus a share of confiscated cattle. ETHICS-002: The 1888 Rudd Concession was obtained by deception - missionary interpreter Charles Helm mistranslated the text, and the verbal assurances given to Lobengula (no more than ten diggers, subject to Ndebele law) were deliberately omitted from the written English version; Lobengula repudiated the concession and protested to Queen Victoria, and was ignored, while Rhodes used it to secure the BSAC royal charter in 1889. ETHICS-002: The Ndebele state itself was built by conquest: Mzilikazi's forces subjugated the Rozvi remnants (c. 1838-1840) and extracted tribute, cattle and captives from western Shona and Kalanga communities, incorporated at the bottom of a three-tier status hierarchy (abeZansi, abeNhla, amaHole). ETHICS-003: the 'predatory raiding state' image is contested - Julian Cobbing and Zimbabwean historians such as Ndlovu-Gatsheni argue it was inflated by BSAC propaganda to justify the 1893 invasion, and this record reports both the violence and the dispute. ETHICS-001: the primary name Mthwakazi is the attested endonym; 'Matabele' is a Sotho-Tswana-mediated exonym adopted by the British and kept only as a variant.
record.chain_notes: Predecessor: Rozvi Empire. Transition violent and two-staged: c. 1835 Nyamazana's Ngoni band (offshoot of Zwangendaba's migration) sacked the Rozvi capital Danamombe and killed Changamire Chirisamhuru, leaving the Rozvi state headless; Mzilikazi's Ndebele, arriving 1838-1840, militarily defeated the Rozvi Mutinhima house, after which the remaining Rozvi royal houses submitted c. 1839-1840 and Nyamazana's Ngoni were absorbed into the Ndebele state (tradition holds she married Mzilikazi). Use c. 1838-1840 for the Rozvi-to-Ndebele link, nature: military conquest plus negotiated submission of remnant houses. Successor: British South Africa Company administration of Matabeleland (later Southern Rhodesia) - violent transition via the First Matabele War: BSAC invasion Oct 1893, occupation of Bulawayo 4 Nov 1893, Lobengula's death Jan 1894, Matabeleland Order in Council 1894; the Ndebele rose again in the Umvukela (Second Matabele War / first Chimurenga) of March 1896 - Oct 1897, suppressed by the BSAC and imperial troops.
record.caveats: Boundary is an honest approximation of the core highveld settlement zone only; the Ndebele state had no linear borders, and its tributary/raiding sphere over western and central Shona country extended far beyond the polygon - this fluidity is the main reason for the 0.65 confidence. year_start 1838 marks the crossing of the Limpopo and settlement in Matabeleland, but the migrant Khumalo polity existed from Mzilikazi's break with Shaka c. 1821-1822, with earlier capitals in the Transvaal; within Matabeleland the capital moved (Mhlahlandlela and Inyathi under Mzilikazi; koBulawayo founded 1870 by Lobengula at the Old Bulawayo site whose verified coordinates are used here; relocated c. 1881 to the site of modern Bulawayo, ~15 km north). year_end 1893 = BSAC occupation of Bulawayo; Lobengula died Jan 1894 (date and smallpox cause reported but debated in Ndebele tradition), and some sources extend the polity to 1894 or to the 1896-97 rising. Wikidata Q1193853 conflates the ethnic group and the polity; Q1266775 is the modern region, not this state. Ndebele casualty figures for Shangani and Bembesi are company-side estimates and likely imprecise.

Saudi forces under Saud bin Abdulaziz took Taif (with a massacre of inhabitants), then Mecca in 1803 and Medina by 1804-05; in 1806 they demolished the domed tombs of al-Baqi cemetery in Medina and Jannat al-Mualla in Mecca (including the tomb of Khadijah) as idolatrous. record.chain_notes: Predecessor: pre-pact Emirate of Diriyah (sheikhdom of the Al Muqrin/Al Saud, c. 1446-1744; Wikidata treats it separately as Q56885910) — the 1744 transition was peaceful and internal: the same dynasty under Muhammad ibn Saud (emir from 22 February 1727) transformed the town emirate into an expansionist state via the pact with Ibn Abd al-Wahhab. Successor: Emirate of Najd (Second Saudi State), founded 1824 when Turki bin Abdullah Al Saud violently retook Riyadh from the Egyptian garrison after a six-year interregnum of Ottoman-Egyptian occupation (1818-1824). The 1818 end was violent: conquest, razing of the capital by Ibrahim Pasha's forces, and execution of the last imam, Abdullah bin Saud, in Istanbul.
record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-002: The state's expansion was overwhelmingly military and accompanied by explicit religious violence. On 21 April 1802 (date disputed, possibly 1801) roughly 12,000 Wahhabi raiders from Najd, sent under Emir Abdulaziz bin Muhammad Al Saud, sacked the Shia holy city of Karbala in Ottoman Iraq, killed an estimated 2,000-5,000 inhabitants, plundered the shrine of Imam Husayn and destroyed its dome — an atrocity still central to Shia collective memory. In 1803 Saudi forces massacred inhabitants of Taif, and after taking Mecca (1803) and Medina (1804-05) they demolished the venerated tombs of al-Baqi cemetery and Jannat al-Mualla in 1806, destruction condemned across much of the Muslim world. The state itself was destroyed by comparable violence: the Ottoman-Egyptian army of Ibrahim Pasha besieged Diriyah for months in 1818, razed the city in 1819, and beheaded the captured Imam Abdullah bin Saud in Istanbul. ETHICS-001: the primary name is the attested Arabic إمارة الدرعية; "First Saudi State" (الدولة السعودية الأولى) is a retrospective label, and the 2022 Saudi royal decree moving the official founding from the 1744 Wahhabi pact back to Muhammad ibn Saud's 1727 accession is a politicized modern re-dating that de-emphasizes the state's Wahhabi origins — both dates are documented here rather than arbitrated. Non-Western historiography is represented via the contemporary Najdi chronicle of Ibn Bishr; Shia accounts of Karbala provide the victims' perspective against Najdi court chronicles that celebrate the raid.
record.caveats: Boundary is an honest approximation of the Najd core only: frontiers were fluid zones of tribal allegiance and tribute collection, never demarcated lines, and the c. 1805-1811 maximum extent (Hejaz, al-Hasa/Gulf coast, Asir, raiding into Iraq, Syria and Oman) lay far beyond this polygon — hence the reduced confidence_score. The Karbala sack is dated 1801 by some scholars and 1802 by others (Vassiliev argues for 21 April 1802). year_start 1744 follows the historiographical consensus (Diriyah Pact); the Saudi state's official 2022 re-dating to 1727 (Muhammad ibn Saud's accession) is documented in chain_notes and ethical_notes. year_end 1818 refers to the 9 September 1818 surrender; the physical razing of Diriyah was completed in 1819. Casualty figures for Karbala (2,000-5,000) and Taif are contemporary estimates, not verified counts.

record.chain_notes: Predecessor: Kingdom of Nepal / Gorkha Kingdom (DB entity ends 2008; founded by Prithvi Narayan Shah's conquests from 1768). Transition: exactly 28 May 2008, when the newly elected 1st Constituent Assembly, at its first sitting, abolished the 240-year Shah monarchy and declared a federal democratic republic by a vote of 560-4; King Gyanendra left Narayanhiti Palace peacefully on 11 June 2008. Transition_type discussion: REVOLUTION fits better than REFORM. Although the terminal act (a parliamentary vote) was procedural and non-violent, it was the direct outcome of the violent 1996-2006 Maoist 'People's War' (~13,000-17,000 dead) plus the April 2006 Jana Andolan II mass uprising (19 days, ~18-25 protesters killed by royal security forces), which forced King Gyanendra to surrender absolute power; the change was a fundamental replacement of the state form (Hindu monarchy to secular federal republic), not incremental reform within the old order. Recommended: REVOLUTION, with the note 'violent insurgency + peaceful mass movement; abolition itself enacted peacefully by elected assembly'. Intermediate steps: Comprehensive Peace Accord 21 Nov 2006; Interim Constitution 15 Jan 2007 (monarchy suspended); CA election 10 April 2008.
record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-002: The republic was born from the 1996-2006 civil war launched by the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) against the Kingdom of Nepal: approximately 13,000 deaths documented by OHCHR (Nepal Conflict Report, 2012), with Nepal government figures reaching ~17,000; INSEC data attribute the majority of documented killings to state security forces (Royal Nepal Army and police, 8,200+ killed 1996-2005) versus 4,000+ killed by the Maoists — both perpetrators named explicitly. ETHICS-002: Over 1,300 people were forcibly disappeared during the war, most by state forces, with Tharu victims of Bardiya district grossly overrepresented; transitional justice (TRC and Commission on Enforced Disappearances) has delivered near-total impunity to date. ETHICS-002: During the September 2015 constitution promulgation, police killed more than 50 Madhesi and Tharu protesters in the Terai (Human Rights Watch documented excessive and unnecessary lethal force; no senior official held accountable), and the subsequent 135-day border blockade (Madhesi groups, partially supported by India) caused a humanitarian fuel and medicine crisis. ETHICS-003: Madhesi, Tharu, Janajati and Dalit communities contest the 2015 federal province boundaries and citizenship clauses as perpetuating historic domination by hill high-caste (Khas Arya) elites; this record documents the dispute without arbitrating it. ETHICS-001: the primary name is the attested Nepali Devanagari form; note the 2015 Constitution (Art. 4) formally names the state simply 'Nepal', while the full republican formula remains in official and international use since 2008. ETHICS-003: the Kalapani-Lipulekh-Limpiyadhura territory (~335-372 km2) is claimed by Nepal (2020 constitutional map amendment) but administered by India — both versions are noted, neither endorsed.

territory_changes.description: On 28 May 2008 the 1st Constituent Assembly, elected on 10 April 2008 under the Comprehensive Peace Accord (21 Nov 2006), abolished the 240-year Shah monarchy by a 560-4 vote and declared the Federal Democratic Republic. The peaceful vote was the direct outcome of the 1996-2006 Maoist civil war (~13,000-17,000 dead; state forces the larger documented killer) and the April 2006 Jana Andolan II mass uprising, in which royal security forces killed ~18-25 protesters before King Gyanendra capitulated.

Constitution of Nepal promulgated 20 September 2015 (domestic constitutional compact, not an international treaty): unitary state restructured into 7 federal provinces. Promulgation was met by months of Madhesi and Tharu protests in the Terai against province boundaries and citizenship clauses; police killed 50+ protesters (HRW-documented excessive force), followed by a 135-day border blockade (Sept 2015-Feb 2016) by Madhesi groups with partial Indian support.

Constitutional amendment (June 2020) added the India-administered Kalapani-Lipulekh-Limpiyadhura triangle to Nepal's official map and coat of arms. This is a cartographic-legal claim only: India continues to administer the territory and rejects the claim. No change of actual control occurred; the dispute remains open.

territory_changes.description: Mahdist forces invaded the Nuba-mountains kingdom of Taqali from 1883, penetrating further than any previous power; in July 1884 its ruler Makk Adam was captured and later died in Mahdist captivity, ending Taqali's ~130 years of independence (DB predecessor entity, ends 1884).

Fall of Khartoum, 26 January 1885: Muhammad Ahmad al-Mahdi's army stormed the city after a long siege; General Charles Gordon was killed and much of the garrison and population massacred. The Turco-Egyptian administration collapsed and the Mahdist state was established with its capital at Omdurman. The Mahdi died 22 June 1885; Khalifa Abdallahi ibn Muhammad ruled 1885-1898/99.

Battle of Gallabat (Metemma), 9-10 March 1889: the Mahdist army under Zeki Tummal repelled Emperor Yohannes IV's Ethiopian invasion force; Yohannes was mortally wounded and his head sent to Omdurman. The eastern frontier stabilized with no lasting territorial change; the same year the Battle of Toski (August 1889) destroyed Wad al-Nujumi's invasion of Egypt and ended northward expansion.

Anglo-Egyptian reconquest under Kitchener: Dongola taken 1896, Atbara April 1898, then Omdurman 2 September 1898, where Maxim guns and artillery killed roughly 10,000-12,000 Sudanese soldiers against 48 dead in Kitchener's force. The state was extinguished and the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium imposed (January 1899); Khalifa Abdallahi was hunted down and killed at Umm Diwaykarat on 24-25 November 1899.

record.chain_notes: Predecessor (main): Turco-Egyptian Sudan under the Khedivate of Egypt — overthrown violently by the Mahdist revolt begun on Aba Island in 1881; the transition completed with the storming of Khartoum on 26 January 1885 (Gordon killed). Predecessor (DB chain, Taqali): the kingdom of Taqali in the Nuba Mountains, independent for ~130 years, was invaded by Mahdist forces from 1883; its ruler Makk Adam was captured in July 1884 and died in captivity — violent conquest, Taqali entity ends 1884 (it re-emerged only as a client under the Condominium after 1889/1898). Successor: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan — violent transition via the British-led reconquest of 1896-1899 (Dongola 1896, Atbara April 1898, Omdurman 2 September 1898); Condominium Agreement signed 19 January 1899; last Mahdist field army destroyed and Khalifa Abdallahi killed at Umm Diwaykarat, 24-25 November 1899.
record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-001: the primary name is the attested Arabic al-Dawla al-Mahdiyya (الدولة المهدية); the dismissive British colonial label "Dervish Empire" is recorded only as a variant. ETHICS-002: the state was born and destroyed in explicit violence. Mahdist forces conquered the Nuba-mountains kingdom of Taqali (1883-84; its ruler Makk Adam died in Mahdist captivity) and stormed Khartoum on 26 January 1885, killing General Gordon and massacring much of the garrison and inhabitants. Under Khalifa Abdallahi the famine of 1888-92 — drought compounded by the Khalifa's own policies, including the crushing of grain-farming communities and mass forced migrations — killed perhaps a third or more of the population; combined famine, war and epidemics reduced Sudan from roughly 7-8 million people to 2-3 million by 1899. At Gallabat/Metemma (9-10 March 1889) the Mahdist army under Zeki Tummal killed Ethiopian Emperor Yohannes IV and sent his head to Omdurman. ETHICS-002 (colonial violence, perpetrator named): the state was annihilated by the British-led Anglo-Egyptian reconquest under Herbert Kitchener — at Omdurman (2 September 1898) Maxim machine guns and artillery killed roughly 10,000-12,000 Sudanese soldiers, many wounded shot where they lay, against 48 dead on Kitchener's side; Kitchener then had the Mahdi's tomb shelled and desecrated, the body exhumed, beheaded and thrown into the Nile, keeping the skull. In Sudanese historiography the Mahdiyya is remembered not as the fanatical "dervish" horde of British accounts but as the first independent Sudanese national state and a foundation of twentieth-century anticolonial nationalism.
record.caveats: Boundaries are an honest approximation: effective control fluctuated sharply — Darfur saw repeated revolts (e.g. Abu Jummayza 1888-89), Equatoria and Bahr al-Ghazal were raided rather than administered, and Suakin and the Wadi Halfa frontier were never held, so the polygon shows the core c. 1886-1896 (Dongola itself was lost to the reconquest in 1896). year_start 1885 dates the state from the fall of Khartoum; the revolt itself began in 1881, and some periodizations use 1881-1898. year_end 1899 follows Wikidata and the Condominium Agreement/death of the Khalifa (November 1899), though effective rule ended with Omdurman in September 1898. Casualty figures at Omdurman vary by source (from ~3,000 to ~12,000 Mahdist dead; ~10,000-12,000 killed is the most commonly cited academic range), and population-collapse figures (7-8M to 2-3M) are rough contemporary estimates, not census data. The famine death toll ("a third or more") is an estimate; sources agree only that losses were catastrophic.

record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-001: the primary name is the attested Tigrinya ምድሪ ባሕሪ ('Land of the Sea'); መረብ ምላሽ (Mereb Melash, 'Beyond the Mereb') reflects the Ethiopian imperial viewpoint and is kept as a variant, while 'Eritrea' is an Italian colonial name (from Greek Erythra Thalassa) imposed by royal decree n. 6592 on 1 January 1890. ETHICS-002: the Ottoman Empire under Ozdemir Pasha conquered Massawa and Hirgigo in 1557 and occupied Debarwa, permanently severing the highlands from the sea; Egypt invaded in the 1870s and was defeated by Yohannes IV at Gundet (1875) and Gura (1876); Ras Alula imprisoned the last hereditary chief Woldemichael Solomon in 1879; Italy under Gen. Baldissera occupied Asmara on 3 August 1889 and proclaimed the Colonia Eritrea in 1890 — the colonizer is named explicitly. The polity's political status is a live scholarly dispute this record deliberately does NOT resolve: Ethiopianist historiography (Pankhurst 1997; Taddesse Tamrat) treats Medri Bahri/Mereb Melash as a tributary frontier province of the Ethiopian Empire whose Bahr Negash owed tribute (e.g., Bahr Negash Dori to Emperor Lebna Dengel, witnessed by Alvares in 1520), while post-independence Eritrean nationalist historiography treats it as an autonomous kingdom and evidence of precolonial Eritrean statehood — a politicization documented by Reid (2014); entity_type 'polity' was chosen to avoid arbitrating between 'kingdom' and 'province'. In the Ethiopian-Adal war the region was overrun by Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi's forces in 1535, and Bahr Negash Yeshaq's 1541 appeal to the Portuguese helped bring Cristovao da Gama's 400-man force to Ethiopia's aid; the same Yeshaq later allied with the Ottomans against Emperors Minas and Sarsa Dengel and died in battle in 1578 — evidence of situational autonomy cited by both sides of the dispute. Provenance: this record exists because ETHICS-018 removed 'Medri Bahri' as an anachronistic name variant of Aksum.
record.caveats: Dating is genuinely uncertain and drives the low confidence: the title baher nagasi may be attested as early as the 12th century (Wikidata gives inception 1137), the conventional start is Zara Yaqob's mid-15th-century reorganization (~1448/1450), and the end is variously placed at 1879 (Ras Alula's Ethiopian absorption), 1889 (Italian occupation of the highlands) or 1890 (colony proclamation); 1450-1890 is a defensible convention, not a certainty. The seat of the Bahr Negash moved from Debarwa, but sources disagree on where and when: some say Tsazega in the 17th century (rise of the Tsazega clan), the current Wikipedia revision says Asmara from 1866 (Gurade Zaray) — Debarwa is kept as capital of record as the longest-attested seat. The boundary is a rough approximation of the core Kebessa plateau only; pre-1557 coastal claims and fluctuating northern/western reach are excluded. Political status (autonomous kingdom vs tributary Ethiopian province) is disputed and unresolved. Confidence 0.55 reflects all four factors.

territory_changes.description: 18 March 1970: National Assembly vote led by Prime Minister Lon Nol and Sisowath Sirik Matak deposed head of state Norodom Sihanouk while he was abroad; the monarchy was abolished and the Khmer Republic formally proclaimed on 9 October 1970. Sihanouk formed the GRUNK government-in-exile allied with the Khmer Rouge, starting full-scale civil war.

April 1970: pogroms against Cambodia's c. 400,000-strong ethnic Vietnamese minority, organized and tolerated by the Lon Nol government — army and police rounded up, interned and massacred thousands of civilians (bodies floated down the Mekong into South Vietnam); most of the surviving community fled or was expelled to South Vietnam.

By the US Congress-mandated bombing halt of 15 August 1973 (end of Operation Freedom Deal), CPK/Khmer Rouge and GRUNK forces controlled most of the countryside; the Republic was reduced to Phnom Penh, provincial capitals and supply corridors. US bombing 1969-73 killed an estimated 50,000-150,000 Cambodian civilians (Kiernan & Owen; disputed range).

17 April 1975: the Khmer Rouge captured Phnom Penh after a siege; the Khmer Republic collapsed and was succeeded by the CPK regime (Democratic Kampuchea). The last government outpost, Preah Vihear temple, fell on 22 May 1975.

record.chain_notes: Predecessor: Kingdom of Cambodia, Sangkum era (DB entity #256, year_start 1953, currently no year_end — should be closed at 1970). Transition: 18 March 1970 parliamentary coup deposing Sihanouk (bloodless in the capital itself, but followed by anti-Vietnamese pogroms and civil war); monarchy formally abolished and republic proclaimed 9 October 1970. Successor: Democratic Kampuchea (DB entity #240, 1975-1979). Transition: violent — Khmer Rouge military conquest of Phnom Penh, 17 April 1975; the CPK regime governed from that date and formally adopted the name Democratic Kampuchea with the 5 January 1976 constitution. This record fills the 1970-75 gap left by the ETHICS-019 fix (record #240 wrongly carried the name of this state).
record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-002: The United States (Nixon administration, US Air Force) bombed the Cambodian countryside in Operations Menu (1969-70) and Freedom Deal (1970 to 15 August 1973), killing an estimated 50,000-150,000 Cambodian civilians per Kiernan and Owen — the toll is disputed, and the underlying tonnage data were themselves revised (c. 2.76 million tons claimed in their 2006 analysis, corrected to roughly 500,000 tons for 1969-73 in their 2015 re-analysis). Shawcross, Chandler and Kiernan all argue the bombing devastated rural society and materially aided Khmer Rouge recruitment. ETHICS-002: In April 1970 the Lon Nol government organized and tolerated pogroms against Cambodia's c. 400,000-strong ethnic Vietnamese minority: army, police and mobs massacred thousands of civilians, whose bodies floated down the Mekong into South Vietnam, and most of the surviving community fled or was expelled. The Khmer Republic was a US-backed military dictatorship whose 1972 presidential election of Lon Nol was widely regarded as rigged, and which survived only on US military and economic aid until the Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975. ETHICS-001: the primary name is the attested Khmer form សាធារណរដ្ឋខ្មែរ (Sathearonaroat Khmae); the French co-official name République khmère is recorded as a variant. This record fills the 1970-75 gap created by the ETHICS-019 correction, under which the Democratic Kampuchea record (#240) had wrongly carried this state's name.
record.caveats: Boundary is the de jure territory (Cambodia's 1970 international borders); de facto control shrank drastically during the civil war — by early 1975 the government held essentially Phnom Penh and besieged enclaves, so any single polygon overstates actual control for 1973-75. The US-bombing civilian death toll (50,000-150,000) is a disputed scholarly range, not a count, and total bomb-tonnage figures were revised between the authors' own 2006 and 2015 publications. The death toll of the 1970 anti-Vietnamese pogroms is attested only as 'thousands'; no precise figure exists. Start year 1970 refers to the 18 March coup; the republic was formally proclaimed 9 October 1970 (Wikidata inception date).

record.boundary_rationale: Polygon represents the pre-Balkan-Wars core of Serbia in its 1878-1912 borders (per task instruction): the Morava valley heartland bounded by the Sava and Danube rivers to the north (Belgrade at the Sava-Danube confluence), the Drina river to the west (border with Austro-Hungarian-occupied Bosnia after 1878), the Timok river and Stara Planina to the east (Bulgarian border; Pirot inside Serbia, Caribrod/Dimitrovgrad outside), and the southern boundary at Ristovac/Presevo south of Vranje, west of Kursumlija along the Kopaonik line (Novi Pazar and the Sandzak remained Ottoman). This includes the four districts (Nis, Pirot, Toplica, Vranje) annexed under the Treaty of Berlin 1878, so it is strictly the 1878-1912 extent, larger than the 1833-1878 principality (which lacked the southeastern districts). It deliberately EXCLUDES the 1913 Balkan-Wars conquests (Kosovo, Vardar Macedonia, Serbian share of the Sandzak), held only 1913-1915 under military/contested rule and never internationally consolidated before the 1915 occupation; that expansion is documented in territory_changes instead. Simplified ~27-vertex polygon, approximate to tens of km; bbox 19.2-23.0 E, 42.3-44.9 N (no antimeridian issues).
record.ethical_notes: ETHICS-002-relevant events, perpetrators named. (1) 1862 Belgrade crisis: after the Cukur Fountain killing of a Serb boy by Ottoman soldiers, the Ottoman garrison bombarded civilian Belgrade from the fortress (~50 killed, hundreds of houses damaged) — perpetrator: Ottoman garrison. The subsequent Great-Power Kanlica conference (1862) mandated the removal of the Muslim civilian population from Serbian towns; ~8,000 Muslims left Belgrade within a year — a state- and Great-Power-sanctioned population removal benefiting the Serbian state, recorded as ETHNIC_CLEANSING with dual agency (Ottoman bombardment; Serbian/Great-Power removal). (2) 1877-78: during and after the Serbian army's conquest of the Nis and Toplica sanjaks, the Muslim population — majority Albanian in the countryside, Turkish in towns, roughly one third of the region's population — was expelled or fled under military pressure; Serbian forces under Prince Milan Obrenovic burned villages and blocked return. Best academic estimates: ~49,000 Albanians among at least 71,000 Muslims (Jagodic 1998; Stefanovic 2005); Albanian historiography cites higher figures. Recorded as ETHNIC_CLEANSING, perpetrator the Serbian army/state. The refugees (muhaxhire) resettled in Kosovo, seeding long-term Serb-Albanian conflict. (3) Balkan Wars 1912-13: Serbian (and Montenegrin) forces conquering Kosovo and Vardar Macedonia committed massacres of Albanian civilians, village burnings and forced conversions, documented contemporaneously by the Carnegie Endowment's 1914 International Commission report — which found grave violations by ALL belligerents (Serbian, Bulgarian, Greek, Ottoman, Montenegrin); Albanians and Macedonian Slavs passed under Serbian rule without consent, under a regime of military administration. (4) WWI 1914-18: Austria-Hungary invaded (perpetrating documented mass executions of civilians in Macva/Sabac in 1914); the 1915 Central Powers conquest was followed by harsh Austro-Hungarian and Bulgarian occupation regimes (internment, forced Bulgarianization in the east, suppression of the 1917 Toplica uprising with mass reprisals); the winter 1915-16 retreat through Albania killed tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians. Serbia's total war losses: 16-28% of the pre-war population depending on methodology (~25% is a common mid-range figure) — among the highest per-capita losses of any WWI belligerent. Serbia in this entry is BOTH perpetrator (1862 removals, 1878 expulsions, 1912-13 conquests) and victim (1862 bombardment, 1914-18 invasion and occupation): both are stated without hierarchy.

territory_changes.region: Pashalik of Belgrade (Sumadija / Morava valley core)
territory_changes.description: Second Serbian Uprising under Milos Obrenovic (from April 1815, Takovo); negotiated settlement with Marashli Ali Pasha gave Serbs de facto self-rule within the Pashalik of Belgrade while remaining under Ottoman suzerainty.

Ottoman hatt-i sharif of 1830 (following the Akkerman Convention 1826 and Treaty of Adrianople 1829) recognized Serbia as an autonomous, tribute-paying hereditary principality under Milos Obrenovic; Ottoman garrisons remained in the fortress towns.

territory_changes.region: Six nahiyes (Krajina, Crna Reka, Banja/Aleksinac, Krusevac, Stari Vlah, Jadar-Radjevina)
territory_changes.description: Supplementary hatt-i sharif of 1833 confirmed the annexation of six contested nahiyes claimed since the First Uprising, enlarging the principality to its 1833-1878 extent.

Cukur Fountain incident: Ottoman soldiers killed a Serb apprentice boy; riots followed and the Ottoman garrison bombarded civilian Belgrade from the fortress (~50 killed). The Great-Power Kanlica conference then mandated the departure of the Muslim civilian population from Serbian towns; ~8,000 Muslims left Belgrade within a year. Dual agency: Ottoman garrison (bombardment); Serbian state and Great Powers (sanctioned population removal).

territory_changes.region: Fortresses of Belgrade, Sabac, Smederevo, Kladovo, Uzice, Soko
territory_changes.description: Ottoman garrisons withdrew from all remaining fortresses; keys of Belgrade fortress ceremonially handed to Prince Mihailo Obrenovic on Kalemegdan (April 1867), ending the Ottoman military presence while nominal suzerainty continued.

territory_changes.region: Nis, Pirot, Toplica and Vranje districts
territory_changes.description: Treaty of Berlin (13 July 1878) recognized Serbia's full independence from the Ottoman Empire and its annexation of four southeastern districts (Nis, Pirot, Toplica, Vranje) taken in the 1876-78 Serbo-Ottoman wars.

territory_changes.region: Nis and Toplica sanjaks (newly annexed districts)
territory_changes.description: During and after the 1877-78 war the Serbian army under Prince Milan Obrenovic expelled the Muslim population of the annexed regions — majority Albanian in the countryside, Turkish in the towns, about one third of the regional population. Academic estimates: ~49,000 Albanians among at least 71,000 Muslims expelled or fled without return (Jagodic 1998; Stefanovic 2005); Albanian historiography cites higher figures. Refugees (muhaxhire) resettled largely in Ottoman Kosovo.

First Balkan War (October-November 1912): Serbian army conquered Kosovo and Vardar Macedonia from the Ottoman Empire. The Carnegie Endowment's 1914 International Commission documented massacres of Albanian civilians, village burnings and forced conversions by Serbian forces, alongside grave violations by all belligerents. Albanian and Macedonian populations passed under Serbian military rule without consent.

territory_changes.region: Kosovo, Vardar Macedonia, eastern Sandzak of Novi Pazar
territory_changes.description: Treaties of London (May 1913) and Bucharest (August 1913) after the Second Balkan War confirmed Serbia's possession of Kosovo, most of Vardar Macedonia (disputed with Bulgaria) and the eastern Sandzak (partitioned with Montenegro), nearly doubling the state's territory. Rule remained contested and militarized until 1915.

TERRITORIAL LOSS: combined Austro-Hungarian, German and Bulgarian offensive (October-November 1915) conquered all of Serbia; the country was partitioned into Austro-Hungarian and Bulgarian occupation zones (internment, forced Bulgarianization, bloody suppression of the 1917 Toplica uprising). The Serbian army and tens of thousands of civilians retreated through the Albanian mountains in winter 1915-16 with mass deaths from cold, hunger and disease; the army was evacuated to Corfu.

Salonika front breakthrough (September 1918) led to the liberation of Serbia by Serbian and Allied forces (Belgrade retaken 1 November 1918). On 1 December 1918 the Kingdom of Serbia merged into the newly proclaimed Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, ending its separate statehood. Serbia's WWI losses were among the highest per-capita of any belligerent (16-28% of pre-war population depending on methodology).

record.chain_notes: Predecessor: Ottoman Empire — DECOLONIZATION, year 1815. Convention chosen: year_start = de facto self-rule, because the entity's own continuous institutions (prince, national chancellery, later assembly) date from the Second Serbian Uprising settlement of 1815; the formal milestones — hereditary autonomy (hatt-i sharif 1830) and full international independence (Treaty of Berlin, 13 July 1878) — are recorded as territory_changes within the entity rather than as separate entity boundaries. Alternative conventions (start 1830 = legal autonomy, or 1878 = sovereignty) are defensible; 1815 follows AtlasPI practice of dating polities from effective self-rule, with the uncertainty made explicit here. Successor: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes — UNIFICATION, 1 December 1918 (proclamation in Belgrade; Serbia's institutions merged into the new South Slav kingdom, Karadjordjevic dynasty continuing). Modeled as ONE entity across the 1882 principality-to-kingdom elevation because state, dynasty context, capital, institutions and international personality were continuous — the proclamation of 6 March 1882 changed the ruler's title, not the state.
record.caveats: (1) Wikidata QIDs given in the task brief were WRONG: Q217106 is 'croquis' (art term) and Q159626 is Wurttemberg. Verified correct items: Q684030 = Principality of Serbia (1815-1882), Q241748 = Kingdom of Serbia (1882-1918). Since AtlasPI models one continuous entity 1815-1918, Q684030 was chosen (matches the primary founding-form name and entity_type 'principality'); consumers needing the kingdom phase should map period 1882-1918 to Q241748 — neither QID alone covers the full span. (2) entity_type 'principality' reflects the founding form; the state was a kingdom for its last 36 years (1882-1918), documented in name_variants and chain_notes. (3) Capital: Kragujevac was the seat of government 1818-1841 (proclaimed capital by Milos Obrenovic; first constitution, school, court founded there); Belgrade — capital from 1841 and the seat of the Sava-Danube confluence fortress — is given as capital as it served for 77 of the 103 years and both founding (1815) and end (1918) phases. (4) WWI loss figures are genuinely contested: direct losses 16-17% (Western estimates) up to 27.6% (Serbian academic estimates); totals including indirect demographic losses (birth deficit, emigration) reach 1.9M/42%. The '~25%' figure in circulation is a mid-range direct-loss estimate. (5) 1878 expulsion numbers contested between Serbian, Albanian and international historiography (30,000 to 70,000+); the figure used (~49,000 Albanians of at least 71,000 Muslims) is the peer-reviewed estimate (Jagodic/Stefanovic). (6) Boundary is the 1878-1912 extent — note it is anachronistic for 1815-1833 (smaller pashalik core) and 1833-1878 (without the four southeastern districts), and excludes the 1913-1915 Balkan-Wars gains; a full temporal-boundary series would need four polygons (1815, 1833, 1878, 1913). (7) Boundary polygon is simplified (~27 vertices, tens-of-km accuracy), hand-traced from river/mountain borders (Sava, Danube, Drina, Timok, Stara Planina), not from a georeferenced historical basemap.
